5. How the models feed the lot tool

Land cover: each lot record has a cover block (building, tree, open ground, hard surface, impervious share, source, date) and the cover inside the suggested spot. Pittsburgh: model:r34_c5_s0, 2022. Philadelphia: landcover_2018. The fit test does not use it. It tells the user how much canopy a unit might remove.
Detector: not used. Lot records carry an empty objects list. Garages and sheds come from building footprints by size (180 sq ft or more is a garage).
Fit: a vector test on the lot outline, edges labeled front, side and rear, building outlines, setbacks from the rule files, and the largest rectangle that fits. See the methods page.

title: MUSA 6950 Results
text:
8. Limits

Land cover scores sit near 0.70 on the held-out counties. The labels set the ceiling.
Philadelphia tree and open ground from NAIP 2022 are not reliable. The 2018 raster misses changes since 2018.
The Pittsburgh per-lot land cover check covers 128 lots.
The detector is not checked against hand labels and is not used in the lot records.
The fit answers are not checked against hand labels.
Lot lines come from county and city parcel maps. They are not a survey. Building outlines can be old or merged.
Rules come from rule files read from the codes. This is not legal advice and not a zoning determination. The bills behind the reform scenarios are not law.
Slope, flood and historic flags are shown but do not change the fit answer.

title: MUSA 5500 Results
text:
Introduction

HB 2186 would allow an ADU (backyard home) on every home lot in Pennsylvania. SB 1346 would do the same outside Philadelphia and Pittsburgh. Both die on Nov 30, 2026 if not enacted
Legal does not mean built. Philadelphia has allowed ADUs in parts of the city since 2012 and only about 10 were built legally
This half of the project asks four things

Where are people and jobs growing?
Did that change after 2019?
Where would a new ADU pay for itself?
How many ADUs could be built by 2031, under today’s rules and under the state bills?

Unit: 2020 census tracts (3,445) and towns (2,572 county subdivisions)

title: MUSA 5500 Results
section: What changed since the first draft
text:
What changed since the first draft

One payoff number. The first draft priced a 600 sq ft unit with the all-unit tract median rent and found 20.3% of tracts pay. The tool used a 1-bedroom rent and showed 10.3%. A 600 sq ft unit is a 1-bedroom, so the 1-bedroom rent is the honest basis. The report now uses the tool’s column. The answer is 10.3% of tracts. The all-unit number is kept as a cross-check
Trend groups. The first draft used K-means with k = 5. Rerun with 20 seeds, k = 5 gives different groups each time (adjusted Rand 0.38). The new rule picks k = 7, which is stable (0.95). All k have weak structure, so the groups are now called a description, not a finding
Forecast. The model is compared with a baseline, ridge and gradient boosting, under county and grid block cross-validation, with a temporal backtest and 90% intervals. Gradient boosting has the lowest held-out error and replaces the random forest. The ADU totals fall because fewer tracts pass the payoff test
ACS windows. “Before” and “after” now say which 5-year windows they compare. Tract changes smaller than their margin of error are flagged
IRS migration was downloaded but unused. It is now tested as a model feature (no gain, so not kept) and shown as a context map
Lots with room. The forecast used the retired raster pilot: one fit rate per area type times ACS single-family homes. It now uses the lot tool’s vector results in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh (measured, every 1 to 4 unit lot) and a model trained on them everywhere else, with a range (section 9)
Town rules. The 12-town list is replaced by the town rule files: 38 municipalities with a rule file, each mapped to a legal class. Every other town is “unknown” (section 9)

title: MUSA 5500 Results
text:
Methods (short)
Full detail is in methods. In short:

Growth: ACS 2010-14, 2015-19 and 2020-24 on 2020 tracts (block crosswalk), dollars in 2024 terms (CPI-U), margins of error from the Census summary files. Jobs from LODES
Groups: six growth rates, standardized. k from 2 to 10 scored by silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, gap and stability. K-means vs Gaussian mixture vs Ward
Payoff: 600 sq ft 1-bedroom unit, $175 / $250 / $300 per sq ft plus 15%, all borrowed for 30 years at 6.53%, 30% of rent to running costs
Forecast: housing growth 2010-20 by tract, models scored with spatial block CV and a temporal backtest. ADUs by 2031 = people x permit rate x payoff x lots x demand x town rule

Demand: job growth slowed after 2019 across most of PA. Real rent growth slowed too. Most single-tract changes are inside the ACS margin of error, so tract stories need care
Groups: tracts do not fall into natural clusters. Seven stable K-means groups summarize the spread. One (478 tracts) saw real rents rise fast in the latest five years
Payoff: a new 600 sq ft 1-bedroom unit pays for itself at $250 / sq ft and 6.53% in about 10% of tracts, mostly around Philadelphia. Build cost matters more than the rent guess or the rate
Why not today: in Philadelphia the law is the binding limit. In Pittsburgh every lot has a legal path and the yard is the limit. 17 of the 36 largest other towns have no ADU text
Room: measured lot by lot, 7.6% of Philadelphia lots and 45.9% of Pittsburgh lots have room for a 600 sq ft unit under state-reform setbacks. Elsewhere the model gives about 2.9 million lots with room (1.5 to 3.6 million), and most of that is extrapolation beyond the two cities
Forecast: housing growth is only modestly predictable (held-out R2 about 0.2 over ten years, about 0.02 over five). Under HB 2186 the stated assumptions give about 13,500 ADUs by 2031 (6,500 to 20,400). Under today’s rules, about 1,000, and that number rests on the 71% of people in towns whose code has not been read

The project
An accessory dwelling unit (ADU) is a small second home on a house lot: a backyard cottage, a unit over a garage, or an apartment inside the house. Two Pennsylvania bills would open ADUs statewide, HB 2186 and SB 1346. Philadelphia has its own bill, 250042. None of them is law. The state session ends Nov 30, 2026.

Does it pay off? Itemised build costs and local rents, and a tract-level test of where a unit covers its loan.

title: MUSA 5500 Proposal
text:
Sent by email to the course staff, Nov 5, 2026. The text below is the proposal as sent.
What changed since: the housing growth model is gradient boosting, picked from four models under county-held-out cross-validation (the proposal named a random forest). The payoff test uses a 1-bedroom rent. The lot tool shows three rule scenarios on each lot in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh: today’s law, local reform and state reform. See Results.
Topic: Housing Demand and ADU Potential Across Pennsylvania
Team: one student
Background: A state bill, HB 2186, would allow a backyard home (ADU) on every home lot in Pennsylvania. But legal doesn’t mean built. Philadelphia has allowed ADUs in parts of the city since 2012, and only about 10 have been built legally. ADUs get built where demand is growing and the rent covers the cost.
Research question: Where are people and jobs growing, did that change after 2019, where would an ADU pay off, and how many could be built by 2031?
Study area: All of Pennsylvania, from 2010 to the latest year, by census tract.
Goal: Planners can see where housing demand is growing and how many new homes ADUs could add in their town or county. Builders and homeowners can search an address and see whether an ADU would pay off there.
Data sources: Census population estimates and ACS through the Census API. IRS migration, LEHD jobs, the Building Permits Survey, and Freddie Mac mortgage rates through scripted downloads. NLCD land cover rasters, OpenStreetMap, and lot counts from my 6950 project (or a simpler estimate from lot sizes if those aren’t ready).
Methods:

Join all the data to census tracts.
Compare growth before and after 2019.
Group places by trend with K-means.
Measure developed land from the rasters and job access with OSMnx.
Test where ADU rent covers the cost to build.
Use a random forest to predict where housing grew from 2010 to 2020, then use it to estimate how many ADUs could be built by 2031, with a low and high range.

Expected outcomes: A multi-page Quarto site on GitHub Pages with interactive maps, a time slider from 2010 to today, and a toggle between current rules and HB 2186. A short written report and a presentation.
Course requirements: API collection, 3+ data sources, spatial joins, OSMnx, K-means clustering, raster analysis, and a scikit-learn model, plus interactive visualizations.
How it splits from 6950: My 6950 project uses AI on aerial images to find which lots have room for an ADU. This project covers demand and payoff. The two will share one dashboard, but each has its own code and documentation pages.

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
text:
The logic lives in Python modules in pipeline/tract/. The notebooks in musa5500/notebooks/ load the data, call the modules and show the result. Every assumption (costs, rates, permit rates, weights, CPI) is read from shared/assumptions.json. The tract keys start with tract..
Run them in that order. Tests: python -m pytest tests -q -k tract.

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
text:
1. Put everything on 2020 tracts

Counts (people, housing units): move 2010-tract numbers to 2020 tracts by land-area share, using the Census block crosswalk
Medians (rent, value, income): cannot be added. Use the value from the 2010 tract with the biggest overlap
Margins of error move the same way. Counts: sqrt(sum((weight x margin)^2)). Medians: the margin of the biggest-overlap tract
Towns: tracts are split into towns with the LODES block crosswalk, weighted by workers who live in each block (LODES 2024)
Inflation: ACS dollars are in the last year of each window. CPI-U yearly averages (2014 = 236.736, 2019 = 255.657, 2024 = 313.689) move them to 2024 dollars. Notebook 01 shows nominal and real values side by side

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
text:
2. Growth before and after 2019
ACS 5-year estimates describe a window, not a year. The three windows are 2010-14, 2015-19 and 2020-24. Their midpoints are 2012, 2017 and 2022.

Before = 2010-14 to 2015-19 (about 2012 to 2017)
After = 2015-19 to 2020-24 (about 2017 to 2022). This step starts two years before 2019, so read it as “the latest five years”, not “since 2019”
Jobs (LODES) are yearly counts. Before = 2010 to 2019. After = 2019 to 2024
Yearly rate = (end / start)^(1 / years) - 1. ACS steps are 5 years between midpoints
Change in trend = growth after - growth before. Positive = sped up
A rate is blank if the start is under 200 people, 100 homes or 50 jobs (tract.growth.min_start)

Margins of error:

The first download kept estimates only. The Census API now refuses calls without a key, so margins come from the public summary files (2010-14 and 2015-19 sequence files, 2020-24 table files). Their estimates match the API values exactly
ACS margins are at 90%. The margin of a difference between two windows is sqrt(m1^2 + m2^2)
Each tract gets flags in trends_tract.csv: *_before_within_moe, *_after_within_moe, *_change_within_moe. True means the change is smaller than its margin, so the data cannot tell it from no change
The “change” flag tests the change in the 5-year change (2020-24 minus twice 2015-19 plus 2010-14)

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
text:
3. Trend groups

Features: growth before and after for jobs, population and real rent
Clip each feature to its 1st and 99th percentile, so a few tiny tracts do not get their own group
Scaling check: raw jobs rates have a standard deviation of 4.8 points a year, population before 2019 only 1.7. The two jobs rates hold 53% of the raw variance. So StandardScaler is used. Without it jobs would decide the groups
k from 2 to 10: inertia (elbow), silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz and the gap statistic (10 uniform reference sets)
Stability: adjusted Rand index (ARI) between K-means runs with 20 seeds, and between the full fit and 20 fits on 80% subsamples
At the chosen k, K-means is compared with a Gaussian mixture (full covariance) and Ward clustering
Rule for k, stated before looking at the groups: keep k where the subsample ARI is at least 0.8 and no group holds under 2% of tracts. Among those, take the best silhouette
Names come from the group medians. The head word is Growing, Steady or Shrinking, from the mean of the jobs and population rates after 2019 (above +0.5% a year, below -0.5%, or in between). Then the measure that stands out most (largest median z-score, at least 0.5), for example “jobs jumped after 2019”
The structure is weak at every k (see results). The groups are a description of the data, not natural clusters
Output: trend_group in trends_tract.csv

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
text:
4. Land and job access
Notebook 03_land_access.ipynb (unchanged)

Developed land: share of each tract in NLCD classes 21-24, for 2010, 2019, 2025, with rasterstats.zonal_stats(..., categorical=True)
Jobs within 30 minutes by car from each tract center, OSMnx drive network, Dijkstra with a 1800 s cutoff, LODES 2024 block jobs. Philadelphia only. Harrisburg could not be downloaded on the run day
Output: data/processed/access_tract.csv

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
section: 5. Does a backyard unit pay off?
text:
5. Does a backyard unit pay off?

Unit: 600 sq ft, one bedroom (tract.payoff.size_sqft)
Cost: $175 / $250 / $300 per sq ft (low / mid / high) plus 15% soft costs, all borrowed over 30 years
Rate: 6.53%, the 2026 average of weekly Freddie Mac rates (financing.pmms30_2026_avg). The sensitivity table adds 7.18%, the latest week (financing.pmms30)
Monthly payment: pipeline.money.loan_payment, the same formula the lot-level money model uses
Net rent = rent x (1 - 30%) for vacancy, repairs, tax and insurance
yes = net rent covers the payment at the mid cost. maybe = it covers the payment at the low cost, or is within 10% of the mid payment. no = anything else

Rent basis. A 600 sq ft unit is a one-bedroom, so the test uses a one-bedroom rent:

Headline: rent_b1 = tract median gross rent (ACS 2020-24, B25064) x the county ratio of 1-bedroom to all-unit median rent (B25031). Where a tract has no median rent, the county 1-bedroom median. The tool uses the same column, so the report and the tool give one number
Cross-check 1: the raw tract 1-bedroom median (B25031). It is blank in about a third of tracts and noisy where it exists
Cross-check 2: HUD Small Area Fair Market Rent, FY2026, 1 bedroom, by ZIP. Each tract takes the mean over its ZIPs, weighted by workers who live in each block. A ZIP in two metro areas takes the lower rent. SAFMRs are the 40th percentile of recent movers, so they run higher than ACS medians, which include long-time tenants
Cross-check 3: the all-unit tract median (B25064), the basis of the first draft
ACS gross rent is top-coded at $3,501, so the richest tracts tie
Outputs: payoff_tract.csv (the tool reads rent_est, cost_month, pays), and in processed/5500/: payoff_summary.json, payoff_sensitivity.csv, payoff_bases.csv, payoff_county.csv

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
section: 6. Where did housing grow? Model and validation
text:
6. Where did housing grow? Model and validation

Target: log(decennial homes 2020 / decennial homes 2010) per 2020 tract, crosswalked. Tracts with under 100 homes in 2010 are left out (3,394 tracts remain)
Features, all from 2010: decennial homes, homes per km2, LODES jobs and workers living in the tract, jobs per home, NLCD developed and high-intensity shares, land area, tract center (x, y)
Extra feature tested: county net migration from IRS files (see 7)
Models: the training-fold median (baseline), ridge regression, random forest (400 trees, 5 per leaf), and histogram gradient boosting with absolute-error loss. A few crosswalk artifacts have log changes past -2, and squared-error boosting chased them
Spatial cross-validation, 5 folds: whole counties held out, and 40 km grid blocks held out. Random 5-fold CV is shown only to show how much it flatters. A test checks that no county or block is on both sides of a split
Rule: the model with the lowest county-held-out MAE is used. R2 is shown too, but the few artifacts dominate it
Temporal backtest: train on the change from 2010-14 to 2015-19 (ACS homes, features at 2010-14), predict the change from 2015-19 to 2020-24 (features at 2015-19), and score against the 2020-24 ACS. Baselines: each tract keeps its own earlier change (last-period rate), and the earlier median. A second score uses only tracts whose change is bigger than its margin of error
No pre-2010 decennial homes are in the data, so the last-period baseline exists only in the backtest
Prediction intervals: split conformal at 90%. The half-width is a high quantile of the absolute county-held-out errors. Coverage is checked fold by fold, with the half-width taken from the other folds only. Quantile gradient boosting (5th and 95th percentiles) is shown for comparison
Feature importance: permutation importance (drop in R2) on held-out counties, averaged over folds. Partial dependence for the top 4 features
The fitted model is fed 2020 values (decennial 2020 homes, LODES 2019, NLCD 2019) to predict 2020-30 growth, with the conformal interval

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
text:
7. IRS migration

County inflow and outflow files from IRS Statistics of Income, 2010-11 to 2022-23. People = exemptions on returns that moved
Net movers per 1,000 residents per year, by county, for 2012-19 and 2020-23 (labels are the second filing year)
Used two ways. As a county feature in the model (flows just after the base year), kept only if it adds more than 0.02 to the held-out R2. It did not, so the model leaves it out. And as a context map of net migration before and after 2019

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
text:
8. ADUs by 2031

ADUs = people x permit rate x payoff weight x lots index x demand x town rule x 5 years, capped at lots with room

Permit rate: 26 / 53.5 / 81 ADU permits per 100,000 people per year (low / mid / high), from cities that allow ADUs by right. The range comes from the proposal, credited to Pew. The exact page still needs to be recorded
Payoff weight: yes 1.0, maybe 0.5, no 0.2 (some people build for family, not rent)
Lots index: lots with room for a 600 sq ft unit per home, over the state ratio, capped at 2. From room_tract.csv (step 12): measured lot by lot in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh, modelled in every other tract. The same count caps the ADUs in each tract. The earlier pilot estimate (lots_tract.csv) is kept beside it for comparison
Demand: 0.5 to 1.5 from the rank of predicted 2020-30 growth

Scenarios, tied to the town rule files through town_legal_class.csv (step 13):

Today: each town’s legal class sets its factor (tract.forecast.legal_class_factor): by right 1.0, discretionary, family-only, conversion-only and unknown 0.02 / 0.05 / 0.10, none 0 / 0.005 / 0.01
HB 2186: every town by right, Philadelphia and Pittsburgh included
SB 1346: every town by right except Philadelphia and Pittsburgh, which the Municipalities Planning Code does not reach. They keep today’s class
Both bills die on Nov 30, 2026 if not enacted

This is scenario arithmetic, not a fitted ADU model. Pennsylvania has no ADU permit series to fit or test it on. The Census permit survey does not split out ADUs, and Philadelphia has about 10 legal ADUs since 2012. The model in step 6 only ranks where housing grows. The low to high range shows the assumptions, not statistical error
Outputs: forecast_town.csv (three rows per town: current, hb2186, sb1346. rule_today keeps the old words allowed, limited, not_allowed. legal_class and review are added at the end), forecast_tract_inputs.csv, and in processed/5500/: forecast_*.csv, forecast_summary.json, and forecast_old_vs_new.csv, which reruns the arithmetic with each mix of old and new inputs so every change can be traced

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
text:
9. County roll-up and linked view

county_rollup.csv: one row per county. Tract counts, people, payoff classes, ADUs by scenario and level, lots with room and net migration. Counts are sums of tracts, so they add up to the state totals. The old pilot columns (lots_total, lots_fit) stay. The new room estimate is added at the end (lots_est, lots_room_low, lots_room_mid, lots_room_high, tracts_room_measured, tracts_outside_training_range)
musa5500/figures/tract_explorer.html: an Altair view with cross-filtering. Click counties on the map, brush tracts on the rent vs predicted growth scatter. The trend group bars, the margin histogram and a table of the best 12 tracts follow the selection. The Vega-Lite spec is saved next to it (tract_explorer.vl.json) for embedding

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
section: 10. Link to the lot tool and the town rules
text:
10. Link to the lot tool and the town rules
The tract model says where demand and payoff are. It does not say what the law or the yard allows on one lot. Two other parts of the project answer that, and the Results page puts them side by side.

Lot tool. pipeline/build_lots.py tests every residential lot in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh under three scenarios: today’s law, local reform (Philadelphia Bill 250042, in Pittsburgh the same as today) and state reform (HB 2186). Each lot gets a legal path per ADU type and a vector fit test on lot lines, buildings and streets with the rule setbacks. lots/<city>/stats.json sums the lots: the share with any legal path today, the share where a detached unit fits, and the top reason a detached unit does not fit or cannot grow
Town rules. shared/rules/ has one rule file per town for the 36 largest municipalities after the two cities (by 2020 population, towns_index.json), plus a statewide baseline (pa_statewide.json). Each file records whether the code addresses ADUs (adu.status), with the section and the date checked. The counts in Results are computed from these files
Steps 11 to 13 feed both into the tract work: the lot results become measured room in the two cities and the training data for a statewide room model, and the town files become the forecast’s legal classes

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
text:
11. Lot results rolled up
lot_rollup.py reads lots/<city>/index.parquet (459,998 Philadelphia and 92,081 Pittsburgh lots with 1 to 4 units) and sums 0/1 flags to tract, city and county. Counts are n_*, shares are share_*.

Legal path (legal_<scenario>): an ADU of some type has a path (by right, administrator or special exception). By right (by_right_<scenario>): the best path for any type is by right
Fit at 400, 600, 800 and 1,000 sq ft (fit<N>_<scenario>): a new detached unit of that size fits the scenario’s setbacks, size cap and other limits. Where a scenario bars new detached units (Philadelphia today and under Bill 250042) the fit engine reports no fit, so those shares are 0
Physical room: fit600_state_reform, the 4 ft side and rear setbacks of HB 2186, the loosest any scenario allows. room600 is the old app field (600 sq ft box after today’s setbacks, sheds cleared)
Garage candidates: an accessory building of garage size stands on the lot. garage_conversion_fits: the conversion test passes today
Outputs: data/processed/lots_tract_v2.csv, lots_city_v2.csv, lots_county_v2.csv. Pittsburgh covers the city only, so its county row is part of Allegheny County
Old vs new: the 26,269 Philadelphia pilot lots are matched to the new lots by nearest centroid (within 15 ft, lot areas within 20%), and the old tract estimate is compared with the new counts for the 385 Philadelphia tracts in both

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
section: 12. Room for a unit in every tract (measured and modelled)
text:
12. Room for a unit in every tract (measured and modelled)

Measured: in the two cities, the share of 1 to 4 unit lots where a 600 sq ft detached unit fits under state-reform setbacks. This is physical room, not legality
Modelled: everywhere else, a ridge regression of that share on features every tract has: log homes per km2, shares of homes in 1-unit detached, 1-unit attached and 2 to 4 unit buildings (ACS 2020-24 B25024, from the Census table file, no key), NLCD developed share (2019), and developed m2 per small-building lot. Tracts weigh by the square root of their lot count. Trained on the 482 city tracts with at least 30 lots (373 Philadelphia, 109 Pittsburgh)
Compared with: the lot-weighted mean, the retired pilot rate by area type, and small gradient boosting
Validation: train on one city and predict the other (both ways), and 2 km block cross-validation within the two cities
Range: 90% band from the cross-city errors (half-width 0.218). Tracts with any feature outside the 1st to 99th percentile of the training tracts are flagged, and their band is doubled (a judgment call, because the cross-city error says little about places unlike both cities)
Lots outside the cities: 1-detached + 1-attached + 2-unit / 2 + 3-4 unit / 3.5 homes (ACS). In the two cities this proxy is 9 to 13% above the real lot count (median tract), correlation 0.96 to 0.97
Output: data/processed/room_tract.csv with source (measured or modelled), outside_training_range, the low / mid / high share and count, and the old pilot count beside it

title: MUSA 6950 Proposal
text:
Submitted Nov 3, 2026.
Room for a Backyard Home: Measuring ADU Capacity Across Pennsylvania with GeoAI
Team: one student
Background and Research Question: Pennsylvania needs more housing, but most towns make it hard to build an accessory dwelling unit (ADU), a small second home on a lot, like a backyard cottage. A state bill, HB 2186, would allow one on every home lot. But no one knows how many lots actually have room for one. Backyards also hold a lot of trees, so building there has an environmental cost.
Research question: How many home lots in Pennsylvania have room for a backyard ADU, how many could fit one without cutting down trees, and can AI on aerial images measure this better than building outlines alone?
Study Area: The whole state of Pennsylvania (all 67 counties), with results for every census tract, town, and county.
Goal: Builders and homeowners can type in an address and see if an ADU fits and where. Planners can see how many new homes ADUs could add in their town or county.
Data Sources: Aerial images of the whole state (NAIP, 2022), building outlines (Microsoft), and property lines from counties that share them. For training, I will use land cover maps from Philadelphia and the Chesapeake Bay area, plus a few hundred lots I label by hand.
Proposed AI Methods: First, a U-Net sorts each image into buildings, trees, and open ground, since building outlines alone do not show trees or pavement. I will compare it with a simpler Random Forest model. Second, YOLO finds garages and sheds the outlines miss. Third, a simple rule checks if each lot has an open spot big enough for an ADU, with and without cutting trees. I will test accuracy on lots I labeled myself, then run it statewide.
Expected Outcomes: A model that maps buildings, trees, and open ground, a map of how many lots can fit an ADU, with and without cutting trees, a check of how accurate the AI is, and a dashboard with an address search and a town and county view. I will share the results in a written report and a presentation.
About the Larger Project: This is half of a bigger ADU project. This half asks whether an ADU fits. My MUSA 5500 project asks whether people need housing there and whether an ADU would pay off, using population, job, and rent trends since 2010. Together they show whether there is room for ADUs where people need housing. Both will share one dashboard, but each class will have its own code and documentation.

title: MUSA 6950 Methods
text:
The question: on a given lot in Philadelphia or Pittsburgh, can a backyard home go up, where, and how big? Aerial images answer part of it (trees, open ground, paving, small buildings). Lot lines, building outlines and zoning answer the rest. This page covers how the land cover model was trained and tested, how it was moved to the two cities, the structure detector, and the vector fit test that the lot tool runs.
Code: pipeline/vision/ (land cover), musa6950/yolo/ (detector), pipeline/fit.py (fit test), pipeline/build_lots.py (lot records). The course notebooks in musa6950/notebooks/ hold the first experiments (Random Forest, first U-Net, the old raster fit rule).

title: MUSA 6950 Methods
text:
1. Labels and preparation

173 boxes of 1 km around tract population centers, NAIP 2022 at 0.6 m, 4 bands.
Chesapeake Bay land cover labels (1 m) put on the 0.6 m grid with nearest neighbour. Codes grouped to 4 classes (other, building, tree, open) or 5 (hard surface split from other). See the data page.
Split by county: 122 train, 24 validation, 27 test boxes. The test counties (Cumberland and Centre) were scored only after every choice was made on validation.
Each band is scaled with the mean and spread of the train boxes.

title: MUSA 6950 Methods
text:
2. Baselines

Random Forest (course lab 6): R, G, B, NIR and NDVI per pixel, 500 random pixels per class per box, 100 trees. musa6950/notebooks/02_random_forest.ipynb.
First U-Net (v1): a plain U-Net written in torch (musa6950/unet.py), 256 px tiles, 10 epochs. musa6950/notebooks/03_unet.ipynb.

title: MUSA 6950 Methods
section: 3. U-Net variants and a fair comparison
text:
3. U-Net variants and a fair comparison
All runs below share one recipe and one test. Only the named change differs.

U-Net with an ImageNet ResNet-34 encoder (segmentation_models_pytorch). The first layer takes 4 bands. R, G and B keep the ImageNet weights. NIR starts as the mean of the RGB weights.
Random 384 px crops, 1 in 3 centered on a building pixel. Flips, 90 degree turns, brightness and contrast jitter.
Loss: class-weighted cross entropy plus 0.5 x Dice. AdamW, learning rate 0.0005, warmup, cosine decay over 16 planned epochs, stopped at epoch 14. Batch 12, 400 steps per epoch.
Validation: every labeled pixel of the 24 validation boxes. The best epoch is kept.
Test: every labeled pixel of the 27 test boxes, predicted in 512 px windows with a 64 px margin. Main score with 8 flips and turns averaged and a tree offset picked on validation. A single-pass score is kept too where it was run.

title: MUSA 6950 Methods
text:
5. Transfer to the two cities

City labels: the 2 ft University of Vermont land cover rasters (Philadelphia 2018, Pittsburgh 2019), 7 classes grouped to the 5-class set. “Other” is water.
40 boxes per city, split into train, validation and test (pipeline/vision/city.py).
Two scores per city: zero-shot (r34_c5_s0, no city training) and fine-tuned (ft_c5_<city>, started from r34_c5_s0, learning rate 0.0001, 250 steps per epoch, up to 12 epochs).
Overlap fix: in Pittsburgh 34.8 % of the test box area was also inside train or validation boxes. city.py now keeps boxes apart, and city test scoring leaves out any test pixel inside a train or validation box. Philadelphia had no overlap.
Philadelphia diagnosis (pipeline/vision/city_check.py): class mapping by NDVI, label alignment by shifting, footprint burn-in, flight dates, an NDVI threshold baseline, tree recall by canopy patch size, and per-lot tree and vegetation shares against the label.

6. Land cover per lot

pipeline/vision/infer_lots.py runs the model over every lot tile and sums pixels per lot (processed/<city>/cover.parquet).
pipeline/vision/raster_cover.py does the same from the city rasters, and compares model and raster per lot. Lots inside the city train and validation boxes are left out of the comparison.

Pittsburgh: the zero-shot model r34_c5_s0 (cover_model_r34_c5_s0.parquet).
Philadelphia: the 2018 city raster. Lots built in 2018 or later get a flag, since the raster may show the old use.

pipeline/vision/cover_lookup.py returns the cover inside any polygon. The lot builder uses it to report the tree, open ground and paving inside the suggested spot.

title: MUSA 6950 Methods
text:
7. Structure detector

Ultralytics YOLO11 small, 640 px chips of PEMA 0.5 ft leaf-off imagery, classes garage, shed, other accessory and pool.
Labels are first pass from footprints and OpenStreetMap: every non-main footprint on a residential lot is one object. Shed under 180 sq ft. Garage 180 to 700 sq ft and within 75 ft of a street, alley or service lane. Other accessory for the rest. Pools from OpenStreetMap.
Areas split 70, 15 and 15 percent, so no area is in two splits.
Scored with AP50 per class on the test areas, against the same first-pass labels.
AGPL-3.0, so the code stays in musa6950/yolo/. Only a detections table leaves the folder.

title: MUSA 6950 Methods
section: 8. The fit test in the lot tool
text:
8. The fit test in the lot tool
The fit test is a vector geometry test. It no longer uses a raster box on the U-Net map.

Lot shape. Lot lines are split into edges and labeled front, side and rear. Front is the line facing the nearest street. On a corner lot the shorter street line is the front. Rear lines on an alley are found from alley lines. Each lot gets an edge confidence (high, medium, low).
Rules. The rules for the lot come from the rule files in shared/rules/ for three scenarios: today’s law, local reform (Philadelphia Bill 250042, in Pittsburgh the same as today) and state reform (HB 2186). The bills are not law. Setbacks, size cap, height and approval path come from the rules. Missing setbacks get labeled fallbacks.
Buildable ground. The lot shrinks by each line’s setback. The house is removed with its separation distance around it. Garages and other outbuildings are hard blocks with a 5 ft clearance. Sheds (under 180 sq ft) are soft blocks: the tool reports “fits if the shed goes”.
Largest rectangle. The largest rectangle inside the buildable ground, at the lot’s own angle and offsets of 8 and 45 degrees. Short side at least 12 ft, long side at most 3 times the short side. The tool looks behind the house first and uses the front yard only when nothing fits behind.
Checks. Room in the yard, size cap, minimum size, share of the house, coverage and height. The first failed check is the limiting reason (no room, yard space, size cap and others). A second detached unit is tested where the rules allow two.
Other types. Internal units, attached units and garage conversions are tested from the house and garage outlines. Attached units use the internal test as a stand-in.
Context. Land cover adds tree canopy, open ground, hard surface, impervious share and the trees inside the suggested spot. Slope, landslide, flood and historic flags come from city layers. None of these change the fit answer.

The same test runs in the browser for a unit the user draws (app/src/lib/lot/verdict.ts), on the saved buildable polygon.

pipeline/build_lots.py runs the fit for every lot and every scenario and writes one record per lot, grouped by census tract, plus stats.json, manifest.json and a QA contact sheet of random lots. Stats count shares of lots: any legal path today, detached unit fits at 400, 600, 800 and 1,000 sq ft, the limiting reason, and the same by housing type and zoning district.
